concurrency-threads.tldr:
• Threads share the heap but each has its own stack; only start() creates a new thread — calling run() executes on the caller.
  • Six states: NEW, RUNNABLE, BLOCKED (monitor), WAITING, TIMED_WAITING, TERMINATED.
  • Interruption is cooperative: blocking calls throw InterruptedException and clear the flag, so restore it with Thread.currentThread().interrupt() or propagate.
  • Daemon threads don't keep the JVM alive and skip finally on exit; set an UncaughtExceptionHandler for visibility.
concurrency-threads.body:
A thread is an independent path of execution inside a JVM process. All threads of a process share the heap (objects, static fields, class metadata) but each has its own stack (local variables, call frames, operand stack) and program counter. That sharing is both the power and the danger of concurrency: two threads can touch the same object at the same time.

What a platform thread really costs. A classic Java thread (new Thread) is a thin wrapper over an operating-system thread. Creating one is a system call; each reserves stack memory (-Xss, 1 MB by default on 64-bit Linux, committed lazily); the OS scheduler decides when it runs and switches between threads with a context switch (save registers, swap stacks, often lose CPU cache warmth: roughly microseconds each). That's why we pool platform threads, and why virtual threads (JDK 21) exist.

Three ways to define work

Java
// 1. Extend Thread (rarely a good idea: you spend your only superclass and mix "work" with "how it runs")
class Worker extends Thread {
    @Override public void run() { System.out.println("run on " + getName()); }
}

// 2. Runnable: no result, cannot throw checked exceptions
Runnable task = () -> System.out.println("runnable");
new Thread(task, "worker-1").start();

// 3. Callable<V>: returns a value, may throw checked exceptions (used with executors)
Callable<Integer> job = () -> 6 * 7;
ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2);
Future<Integer> f = pool.submit(job);
System.out.println(f.get()); // 42
pool.shutdown();

// JDK 21: Thread.Builder for platform and virtual threads
Thread platform = Thread.ofPlatform().name("io-", 0).daemon(false).start(task);
Thread virtual  = Thread.ofVirtual().name("vt-", 0).start(task);

Pitfall calling run() directly executes on the current thread — no new thread is created. Only start() creates one, and calling start() twice throws IllegalThreadStateException.

Thread states (Thread.State)

State Meaning How you get there How you leave
NEW created, not started new Thread(...) start()
RUNNABLE running or ready to run (the OS decides) start(), lock acquired, wait finished blocking call, end of run()
BLOCKED waiting to enter a synchronized block held by another thread contended monitor monitor released
WAITING waiting with no timeout Object.wait(), Thread.join(), LockSupport.park() (all j.u.c locks) notify, target thread ends, unpark, interrupt
TIMED_WAITING waiting with a timeout sleep(ms), wait(ms), join(ms), parkNanos, tryLock(timeout) timeout, signal, interrupt
TERMINATED run() finished (normally or by exception) — —

Two details interviewers probe: a thread blocked on I/O (a socket read) shows as RUNNABLE in a thread dump, because from the JVM's view it's executing native code; and a thread waiting for a ReentrantLock shows as WAITING (parking), not BLOCKED — BLOCKED is only for synchronized monitors.

Key Thread methods

Method What it does Notes
start() creates the OS thread and calls run() on it once per thread
join() / join(ms) waits for the thread to finish all its actions happen-before join returns
Thread.sleep(ms) pauses the current thread keeps any locks it holds
Thread.yield() hints the scheduler to run another thread rarely useful; no guarantees
interrupt() sets the target's interrupt flag (and wakes it from blocking calls) cooperative cancellation
isInterrupted() reads the flag doesn't clear it
Thread.interrupted() (static) reads and clears the current thread's flag easy to misuse
setDaemon(true) JVM may exit while it runs before start()
setUncaughtExceptionHandler callback for exceptions escaping run() per thread or default

Interruption is cooperative. t.interrupt() doesn't stop anything by force; it sets a flag. Blocking methods (sleep, wait, join, BlockingQueue.take, lockInterruptibly, Future.get) notice it, clear the flag and throw InterruptedException. Your code must react: either propagate the exception or restore the flag so callers further up can see it.

Java
public void run() {
    while (!Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) {
        try {
            Item item = queue.take();      // blocks; responds to interrupt
            process(item);
        } catch (InterruptedException e) {
            Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); // restore the flag
            break;                              // and exit cleanly
        }
    }
}

Pitfall swallowing InterruptedException with an empty catch makes the thread impossible to stop and silently breaks ExecutorService.shutdownNow() and Future.cancel(true).

Code that never blocks (a CPU loop) must check Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted() itself. Interruption can't break out of synchronized waiting (BLOCKED state) or classic blocking java.io streams — use lockInterruptibly() and NIO channels (which close on interrupt) when cancellation matters.

Stopping a thread the right way: interruption, or a volatile boolean running flag for loops that don't block. Thread.stop() was unsafe (it released all locks mid-update, leaving objects corrupted); it throws UnsupportedOperationException since JDK 20, and suspend/resume were deadlock-prone and have been degraded and removed in recent JDKs.

Daemon threads don't keep the JVM alive: when only daemon threads remain, the JVM exits without running their finally blocks. Use them for background housekeeping (cache cleaners), never for work that must complete (flushing writes, committing offsets).

Priorities (setPriority(1..10)) are hints the OS mostly ignores on Linux; never rely on them for correctness.

Uncaught exceptions kill only the thread they escape from, and the default handler just prints the stack trace to stderr — easy to miss in production. Set a handler (or log inside the task):

Java
Thread t = new Thread(() -> { throw new IllegalStateException("boom"); }, "importer");
t.setUncaughtExceptionHandler((th, ex) -> log.error("{} died", th.getName(), ex));
t.start();
t.join();

// Global default for every thread without its own handler:
Thread.setDefaultUncaughtExceptionHandler((th, ex) -> log.error("Uncaught in {}", th.getName(), ex));

Name your threads. Thread dumps full of Thread-17 and pool-3-thread-2 make incidents slower. Give every pool a ThreadFactory (or Spring's ThreadPoolTaskExecutor.setThreadNamePrefix) so dumps say order-import-3.

Java
ThreadFactory named = Thread.ofPlatform().name("order-import-", 1).factory();   // JDK 21
ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4, named);

concurrency-jmm.tldr:
• Bugs come from atomicity, visibility and ordering; the JMM guarantees visibility only along happens-before edges.
  • Key edges: unlock → next lock, volatile write → later read, start(), join(), and transitivity.
  • volatile gives visibility and ordering, not atomicity: count++ on a volatile still loses updates.
  • Publish shared objects safely: final fields, volatile/atomic references, static initializers or a lock.
concurrency-jmm.body:
Concurrency bugs come from three sources:

  1. Atomicity — an operation you think of as one step is several (count++ is read, add, write) and threads interleave between the steps.
  2. Visibility — a write sits in a CPU core's store buffer or cache, or a register the JIT kept it in, and another core never sees it.
  3. Ordering — the compiler, the JIT and the CPU all reorder instructions when it doesn't change the result for a single thread. Another thread can observe the reordering.

A write by thread A can sit in core 0's store buffer while thread B reads an older value from its own cache; the JIT may also keep a field in a register for an entire loop. The Java Memory Model (JMM) is the contract that tells you when a write is guaranteed to be visible to a read in another thread: when there is a happens-before (HB) relationship between them.

A data race is two accesses to the same variable from different threads, at least one a write, with no happens-before ordering between them. Programs without data races behave as if all operations ran in some sequential order (sequential consistency for data-race-free programs). With races, all bets are off.

Happens-before rules you must know

Rule Guarantee
Program order each action in a thread HB every later action in the same thread
Monitor lock an unlock of a monitor HB every subsequent lock of the same monitor
Volatile a write to a volatile field HB every subsequent read of that field
Thread start t.start() HB every action in t
Thread termination every action in t HB another thread returning from t.join() (or seeing isAlive() == false)
Interruption t.interrupt() HB the interrupted thread detecting it
Final fields a correctly constructed object's final fields are visible to every thread that sees the reference (if this didn't escape the constructor)
j.u.c utilities queue.put HB take; latch.countDown() HB await() return; future completion HB get(); releasing a lock/semaphore HB the next acquire
Transitivity A HB B and B HB C ⇒ A HB C

Publishing data through a volatile flag — the canonical example:

Java
class Publisher {
    private int data;                 // plain field
    private volatile boolean ready;   // the "publication" flag

    void write() { data = 42; ready = true; }       // writer
    void read()  { if (ready) System.out.println(data); }   // prints 42, never 0
}

Remove volatile and the reader may see ready == true but data == 0 (the writes were reordered or not yet visible), or may never see ready change at all.

The classic visibility bug — a loop that never ends

Java
class StopFlag {
    private boolean running = true;          // NOT volatile
    void stop() { running = false; }
    void loop() {
        while (running) { /* busy */ }       // JIT may hoist the read out of the loop: infinite loop
    }
}
// Fix: private volatile boolean running = true;

Reordering you can actually observe

Java
int x = 0, y = 0, r1, r2;
// Thread 1:  x = 1; r1 = y;
// Thread 2:  y = 1; r2 = x;
// Intuition says at least one of r1, r2 is 1. Without synchronization, r1 == 0 && r2 == 0 is allowed
// (and happens on real x86 hardware because of store buffers). Declaring x and y volatile forbids it.

What volatile gives you: visibility and ordering — no reordering of earlier writes after a volatile write (release) or of later reads before a volatile read (acquire); 64-bit long/double writes become atomic. What it doesn't give: atomicity of compound actions.

Java
volatile int count;
count++; // NOT atomic: read -> add -> write. Two threads can both read 5 and both write 6.
         // Use AtomicInteger/LongAdder, or a lock.

Safe publication — an object is safely published when another thread obtains the reference through:

  • a static initializer (static final Config INSTANCE = new Config();),
  • a volatile field or an AtomicReference,
  • a final field of a properly constructed object,
  • a field guarded by a lock that both threads use,
  • a concurrent collection (ConcurrentHashMap.put, BlockingQueue.put).

Anything else risks another thread seeing a partially constructed object: the reference can become visible before the constructor's writes. This is exactly why double-checked locking needs volatile.

Don't let this escape the constructor (registering a listener, starting a thread, or storing this in a static field from inside the constructor): another thread can then see the object before its fields — even final ones — are initialized.

VarHandle access modes (JDK 9+) expose the spectrum explicitly; you rarely need them in application code, but they explain what each level costs:

Mode Guarantees Typical use
plain none across threads single-threaded data
opaque eventually visible, no reordering of accesses to that variable progress flags in lock-free code
release / acquire the publication pattern above, cheaper than volatile lock-free queues, single-writer handoff
volatile release/acquire + total order over all volatile accesses default choice when in doubt

Interview tip "volatile is for flags and for publishing references to immutable or effectively immutable objects; locks are for invariants that span several variables or compound actions." Mention that the JMM bugs are hard to reproduce, so the tool for testing them is jcstress (the OpenJDK concurrency stress harness), not unit tests.

concurrency-synchronized.tldr:
• Every object has a monitor; synchronized gives mutual exclusion plus visibility and is reentrant.
  • Prefer a private final lock object over locking this or the class.
  • Always call wait() in a while loop on the condition, holding the monitor; use notifyAll() when different kinds of waiters share it.
  • sleep keeps locks; wait releases the monitor.
concurrency-synchronized.body:
Every Java object can act as a lock, called its intrinsic lock or monitor. synchronized gives two guarantees: mutual exclusion (only one thread inside the protected region per monitor) and visibility (unlocking happens-before the next lock of the same monitor, so the next owner sees all writes made while the lock was held).

Java
public class Counter {
    private int value;
    public synchronized void increment() { value++; }      // locks `this`
    public synchronized int get() { return value; }        // reads must lock too, for visibility
    public static synchronized void util() { }             // locks Counter.class (a different monitor!)

    private final Object lock = new Object();
    public void add(int n) {
        synchronized (lock) { value += n; }                // explicit private lock object
    }
}

How a monitor works. A monitor has an owner, a recursion count (it's reentrant), an entry set of threads waiting to acquire it (state BLOCKED) and a wait set of threads that called wait() on it (state WAITING).

Under the hood HotSpot keeps lock state in the object header's mark word. An uncontended lock is acquired with a single CAS (a "lightweight" or "thin" lock); only under contention does it inflate to a full ObjectMonitor with OS-level parking. Biased locking (an older optimization) was disabled in JDK 15 and removed in JDK 18. The JIT also applies lock elision (removing locks on objects that never escape the thread) and lock coarsening (merging adjacent locks on the same object).

Properties to state in interviews

  • Reentrant: a thread holding a monitor can enter it again (a synchronized method calling another synchronized method on the same object doesn't deadlock).
  • Not interruptible, no timeout: a thread BLOCKED on a monitor waits until it gets it. Use ReentrantLock for tryLock(timeout) or lockInterruptibly().
  • Block-structured: released automatically when the block exits, normally or by exception, so you can't forget to unlock.
  • Instance vs static: synchronized instance methods lock this; static ones lock the Class object. They don't exclude each other.

What to lock on

Lock object Verdict
private final Object lock = new Object() best: nobody outside can interfere
this (synchronized methods) fine for simple classes, but any caller can also lock your object and cause contention or deadlock
SomeClass.class global for the class: protects static state
String literals, boxed Integers never: they're interned/cached and shared JVM-wide
a non-final field never: reassigning it means threads lock different objects

wait / notify — condition waiting on a monitor. wait() atomically releases the monitor and suspends the thread; notify() moves one waiter (arbitrary) from the wait set back to the entry set; notifyAll() moves all of them. All three must be called while holding the monitor, otherwise IllegalMonitorStateException.

Always wait in a loop, for three reasons: the spec allows spurious wakeups; by the time a notified thread reacquires the monitor another thread may have consumed the condition; and with notifyAll you wake threads waiting for different conditions.

Java
public class BoundedBuffer<T> {
    private final Queue<T> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
    private final int capacity;
    public BoundedBuffer(int capacity) { this.capacity = capacity; }

    public synchronized void put(T item) throws InterruptedException {
        while (q.size() == capacity) wait();   // loop, not if
        q.add(item);
        notifyAll();                           // wake consumers
    }
    public synchronized T take() throws InterruptedException {
        while (q.isEmpty()) wait();
        T item = q.poll();
        notifyAll();                           // wake producers
        return item;
    }
}

Pitfall notify() wakes one arbitrary waiter. When producers and consumers wait on the same monitor, notify() can wake another producer while the buffer is full; it goes back to waiting and nobody wakes the consumers (a lost wakeup). Use notifyAll(), or a ReentrantLock with separate Conditions.

sleep vs wait

Thread.sleep(ms) obj.wait()
Defined on Thread (static) Object
Must hold the monitor no yes
Releases locks no — sleeps while holding them releases that monitor
Wakes on timeout, interrupt notify/notifyAll, timeout, interrupt, spuriously
Purpose pause wait for a condition

Common mistakes: synchronizing only the writer (readers also need the lock for visibility); holding a lock during slow I/O or a remote call (every other thread queues behind it); calling unknown code (listeners, callbacks) while holding a lock (they may take other locks in the opposite order → deadlock); synchronizing on a different object in each method of the same class.

Interview tip on JDK 21–23, a virtual thread that blocks inside synchronized pins its carrier thread; JDK 24 (JEP 491) fixed this. Prefer ReentrantLock around blocking calls if you target older LTS versions with virtual threads.

concurrency-locks.tldr:
• ReentrantLock adds tryLock with timeout, interruptible locking, fairness and multiple Conditions; always unlock in finally.
  • Two Conditions (notFull, notEmpty) give targeted wakeups in bounded buffers.
  • ReentrantReadWriteLock allows many readers or one writer; downgrade is allowed, upgrade deadlocks.
  • StampedLock optimistic reads take no lock but must be validated; it isn't reentrant.

concurrency-atomics.tldr:
• Atomics use CAS retry loops: lock-free, so no deadlocks, but retries waste CPU under heavy contention.
  • LongAdder stripes a counter across cells and beats AtomicLong for write-heavy metrics.
  • ABA: a value changes A→B→A and CAS still succeeds; fix with AtomicStampedReference.
  • updateAndGet lambdas may run several times, so they must be side-effect free.
concurrency-atomics.body:
Atomic classes provide thread-safe single-variable updates without locks, using compare-and-swap (CAS): "set the value to B only if it is still A; tell me whether it worked". On x86 that's one instruction (LOCK CMPXCHG); on ARM a load-linked/store-conditional pair. If another thread changed the value first, the CAS fails and you retry.

Java
AtomicInteger hits = new AtomicInteger();
hits.incrementAndGet();
hits.updateAndGet(v -> Math.min(v * 2, 1000));     // lambda must be side-effect free (may run several times)
hits.accumulateAndGet(5, Integer::sum);

// What incrementAndGet does, conceptually:
int incrementAndGet(AtomicInteger a) {
    int prev, next;
    do {
        prev = a.get();
        next = prev + 1;
    } while (!a.compareAndSet(prev, next));        // retry until we win the race
    return next;
}

Lock-free means some thread always makes progress (no thread can block others by being descheduled while holding a lock), so there are no deadlocks or priority inversion. It doesn't mean free: under heavy contention many CAS attempts fail and threads spin, burning CPU, and every successful CAS bounces the cache line between cores.

The atomic toolbox

Class Use
AtomicInteger, AtomicLong, AtomicBoolean counters, flags, sequence numbers
AtomicReference<V> swap a whole (preferably immutable) object atomically
AtomicIntegerArray, AtomicLongArray, AtomicReferenceArray per-element atomic updates
AtomicLongFieldUpdater etc. atomic updates on a volatile field of many objects without a wrapper per object
AtomicStampedReference, AtomicMarkableReference CAS on reference + version/mark (ABA protection)
LongAdder, DoubleAdder high-contention sums (metrics)
LongAccumulator high-contention custom reductions (max, min)
VarHandle (JDK 9+) low-level atomic and fenced access to fields and array elements; replaces Unsafe

LongAdder — striping to beat contention. Instead of one hot variable, it keeps a base plus an array of padded Cells; a thread that loses a CAS on base moves to its own cell. sum() adds them up.

Java
LongAdder requests = new LongAdder();
requests.increment();          // from many threads: near-zero contention
long total = requests.sum();   // read occasionally; NOT an atomic snapshot while writers run

LongAccumulator maxLatency = new LongAccumulator(Long::max, Long.MIN_VALUE);
maxLatency.accumulate(observedMicros);

Use AtomicLong when you need the exact current value on every update (sequence generators, compareAndSet logic); use LongAdder for counters that are written constantly and read rarely.

The ABA problem. Thread 1 reads A and gets descheduled; thread 2 changes A → B → A; thread 1's CAS succeeds, although the state changed in between. For a counter that's harmless; for a lock-free stack that reuses nodes, it corrupts the structure.

Fix with a version stamp (AtomicStampedReference), or avoid node reuse (in Java the GC guarantees a removed node isn't recycled while someone still references it, which is why ABA is rarer than in C++).

Java
AtomicStampedReference<Node> top = new AtomicStampedReference<>(null, 0);
int[] stampHolder = new int[1];
Node current = top.get(stampHolder);
top.compareAndSet(current, newNode, stampHolder[0], stampHolder[0] + 1);   // fails if the stamp moved

Lock-free stack (Treiber stack) — the classic interview implementation:

Java
public class LockFreeStack<T> {
    private record Node<T>(T value, Node<T> next) {}
    private final AtomicReference<Node<T>> head = new AtomicReference<>();

    public void push(T v) {
        Node<T> oldHead, newHead;
        do {
            oldHead = head.get();
            newHead = new Node<>(v, oldHead);
        } while (!head.compareAndSet(oldHead, newHead));
    }
    public T pop() {
        Node<T> oldHead;
        do {
            oldHead = head.get();
            if (oldHead == null) return null;
        } while (!head.compareAndSet(oldHead, oldHead.next()));
        return oldHead.value();
    }
}

When atomics aren't enough. Two atomics don't make a compound invariant atomic: if (balance.get() >= amt) balance.addAndGet(-amt) is still a check-then-act race. Options: a single CAS loop on one variable (updateAndGet with the check inside), an AtomicReference to an immutable state object that holds all related fields, or a lock.

Java
record Range(int lower, int upper) {}
AtomicReference<Range> range = new AtomicReference<>(new Range(0, 10));

void setLower(int v) {
    range.updateAndGet(r -> {
        if (v > r.upper()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("lower > upper");
        return new Range(v, r.upper());      // both fields change together, atomically
    });
}

Pitfall updateAndGet/accumulateAndGet functions may be called several times under contention. Never put side effects (logging, I/O, incrementing other counters) inside them.

concurrency-executors.tldr:
• ThreadPoolExecutor order: core threads → queue → extra threads up to max → rejection handler.
  • newFixedThreadPool uses an unbounded queue (OOM risk) and newCachedThreadPool unbounded threads: build your own with a bounded queue, named threads and a deliberate rejection policy.
  • Size CPU-bound pools near the core count; I/O-bound ≈ cores × (1 + wait/compute), then measure.
  • submit() hides exceptions inside the Future; shut down with shutdown() + awaitTermination() then shutdownNow().
concurrency-executors.body:
Creating a platform thread per task is expensive (OS thread creation, stack memory, scheduling), and an unbounded number of threads takes the machine down under load. Thread pools reuse a bounded set of threads and queue the excess. The Executor framework separates what to run (tasks) from how it runs (threads, queues, policies).

The 7 parameters of ThreadPoolExecutor — everything in Executors.* is a preconfigured version of this:

Java
ThreadPoolExecutor pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(
    8,                                         // corePoolSize: threads kept alive even when idle
    32,                                        // maximumPoolSize: hard upper bound
    60, TimeUnit.SECONDS,                      // keepAliveTime for threads above core
    new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(500),             // workQueue: BOUNDED
    Thread.ofPlatform().name("order-pool-", 0).factory(),   // name your threads (JDK 21; Guava ThreadFactoryBuilder before)
    new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy()  // what to do when saturated
);
pool.allowCoreThreadTimeOut(true);             // optional: let idle core threads die too
pool.prestartAllCoreThreads();                 // optional: warm up before traffic

What happens when you submit a task (memorize this order)

The surprise for most people: the pool grows beyond core size only after the queue is full. With an unbounded queue it never grows past core and never rejects: the queue just eats memory.

Choosing the queue

Queue Behaviour Used by
ArrayBlockingQueue(n) bounded, array-backed recommended for custom pools
LinkedBlockingQueue() unbounded unless you pass a capacity newFixedThreadPool, newSingleThreadExecutor
SynchronousQueue capacity 0: hand-off to an idle thread or create one newCachedThreadPool
PriorityBlockingQueue ordered by priority, unbounded priority job runners
DelayedWorkQueue ordered by trigger time ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor

The Executors factory traps

Factory Under the hood Risk
newFixedThreadPool(n) core = max = n, unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue the queue grows until OutOfMemoryError; latency hidden in the queue
newCachedThreadPool() core 0, max Integer.MAX_VALUE, SynchronousQueue thread explosion under load
newSingleThreadExecutor() 1 thread, unbounded queue queue OOM
newScheduledThreadPool(n) fixed core size, unbounded delay queue unbounded queue
newWorkStealingPool() ForkJoinPool daemon threads; not for blocking I/O
newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() one virtual thread per task (JDK 21) none of the above; bound downstream resources yourself

Rejection policies

Policy Behaviour When
AbortPolicy (default) throws RejectedExecutionException caller can handle overload (return 503)
CallerRunsPolicy the submitting thread runs the task itself natural backpressure: producers slow down
DiscardPolicy silently drops only for best-effort work (metrics samples)
DiscardOldestPolicy drops the oldest queued task, retries freshest data matters most
custom log, count, persist for retry most production code

Sizing a pool

  • CPU-bound work: threads ≈ cores (maybe +1). More threads only add context switching.
  • I/O-bound work (Goetz): threads ≈ cores × (1 + wait time / compute time). 8 cores, requests that wait 90 ms on I/O for every 10 ms of CPU → 8 × (1 + 9) = 80 threads.
  • Little's law sanity check: concurrent requests in flight = arrival rate × latency. 400 req/s × 0.2 s = 80 requests in flight, so you need ~80 threads (or async I/O / virtual threads).
  • Respect downstream limits: 200 threads calling a database with a 20-connection pool just moves the queue into Hikari.
  • Then load test and watch CPU, queue depth, p99 latency and rejections.

Pool lifecycle and graceful shutdown

Java
void shutdownGracefully(ExecutorService pool) {
    pool.shutdown();                                   // stop accepting new tasks
    try {
        if (!pool.awaitTermination(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) {
            List<Runnable> dropped = pool.shutdownNow(); // interrupt running tasks
            log.warn("Dropped {} queued tasks", dropped.size());
            if (!pool.awaitTermination(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) log.error("Pool did not terminate");
        }
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        pool.shutdownNow();
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
    }
}
// JDK 19+: ExecutorService is AutoCloseable; try (var pool = ...) { } calls close(), which waits for tasks

Exceptions inside tasks — where do they go?

Submitted with Exception ends up
execute(Runnable) thrown on the worker thread → UncaughtExceptionHandler (printed to stderr by default); the worker is replaced
submit(...) captured inside the Future; silently lost unless someone calls get()
scheduleAtFixedRate captured; all future runs are cancelled silently

Always catch and log inside long-running or scheduled tasks, or override ThreadPoolExecutor.afterExecute to log failures centrally.

Scheduling

Java
ScheduledExecutorService ses = Executors.newScheduledThreadPool(2, Thread.ofPlatform().name("sched-", 0).factory());
ses.scheduleAtFixedRate(this::pollMetrics, 0, 10, TimeUnit.SECONDS);    // start-to-start (runs back to back if late)
ses.scheduleWithFixedDelay(this::cleanup, 0, 1, TimeUnit.MINUTES);      // end-to-start (always a gap)
ses.schedule(() -> sendReminder(orderId), 30, TimeUnit.MINUTES);        // one-shot

Monitoring a pool — expose these as metrics (Micrometer's ExecutorServiceMetrics.monitor(registry, pool, "orders") does it):

Signal Meaning when high
getActiveCount() ≈ max saturated
getQueue().size() growing arrival rate > processing rate
rejections > 0 overload reaching callers
task duration p99 rising downstream slowness
getLargestPoolSize() how close to max you've come

In Spring use ThreadPoolTaskExecutor (bounded queue, thread name prefix, TaskDecorator for MDC/security context, graceful shutdown via setWaitForTasksToCompleteOnShutdown(true) and setAwaitTerminationSeconds).

concurrency-completablefuture.tldr:
• thenApply maps, thenCompose flat-maps async calls, thenCombine merges two independent futures, allOf fans in.
  • Always pass your own executor for I/O; the default common pool is small and shared with parallel streams.
  • Handle failures with exceptionally/handle, unwrap CompletionException, and add orTimeout.
  • complete() / completeExceptionally() bridge callback APIs into futures.
concurrency-completablefuture.body:
A Future<V> is a handle to a result that will exist later. Its API is poor: get() blocks, you can't attach callbacks, you can't combine futures, and you can't complete one yourself. CompletableFuture (CF) fixes all of that: it's a promise you can chain, combine, recover from failures and complete manually.

Fan-out / fan-in — the most common production use

Java
ExecutorService io = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(20);  // never rely on the common pool for blocking I/O

CompletableFuture<User> userF          = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> userClient.get(id), io);
CompletableFuture<List<Order>> ordersF = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> orderClient.list(id), io);
CompletableFuture<Integer> pointsF     = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> loyalty.points(id), io);

CompletableFuture<Profile> profileF = userF
    .thenCombine(ordersF, (u, os) -> new Profile(u, os))                  // two independent calls, merged
    .thenCombine(pointsF, Profile::withPoints)
    .orTimeout(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS)                                       // JDK 9+
    .exceptionally(ex -> Profile.fallback(id));                           // recover from any failure above

Profile p = profileF.join();     // total latency ≈ the slowest call, not the sum

Method cheat sheet

Method Input → output Analogy / use
supplyAsync(s, ex) / runAsync(r, ex) start async work
thenApply(fn) T → U map
thenCompose(fn) T → CF<U> flatMap: chain a dependent async call
thenAccept(c) / thenRun(r) consume / side effect
thenCombine(cf, bi) (T, U) → V join two independent futures
allOf(cfs...) → CF<Void> wait for all (then join each)
anyOf(cfs...) → CF<Object> first to complete (hedged requests)
exceptionally(fn) Throwable → T recover
handle(bi) (T, Throwable) → U always runs; map success or failure
whenComplete(bi) (T, Throwable) → same result side effect (logging, metrics)
orTimeout(t, u) fail with TimeoutException JDK 9+
completeOnTimeout(v, t, u) default value on timeout JDK 9+
complete(v) / completeExceptionally(ex) finish it yourself bridging callbacks

thenApply vs thenCompose

Java
CompletableFuture<User> user = findUser(id);                                        // async
CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<Account>> nested = user.thenApply(u -> findAccount(u));   // wrong shape
CompletableFuture<Account> flat = user.thenCompose(u -> findAccount(u));                       // right

Which thread runs each stage? This trips people up.

Variant Runs on
thenApply(fn) (non-async) the thread that completed the previous stage, or the caller's thread if the stage was already complete when you attached it
thenApplyAsync(fn) ForkJoinPool.commonPool()
thenApplyAsync(fn, executor) your executor

So a cheap transformation is fine non-async; anything that blocks or is expensive should use the *Async(…, executor) variant, or it runs on (and blocks) whatever thread happened to complete the previous stage — maybe a Netty event loop or an HTTP client's I/O thread.

How exceptions propagate

A failure skips every following "success" stage until a recovery stage (exceptionally, handle). join() wraps the cause in CompletionException (unchecked), get() in ExecutionException (checked); unwrap with getCause().

Fan-out over a list and collect results

Java
List<CompletableFuture<Price>> futures = skus.stream()
    .map(sku -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> pricing.fetch(sku), io))
    .toList();

CompletableFuture<List<Price>> all = CompletableFuture
    .allOf(futures.toArray(CompletableFuture[]::new))
    .thenApply(v -> futures.stream().map(CompletableFuture::join).toList());   // join won't block: all done

List<Price> prices = all.get(3, TimeUnit.SECONDS);

allOf fails as soon as any future fails, but the others keep running. To tolerate partial failure, attach exceptionally to each future before allOf.

Bridging a callback API

Java
CompletableFuture<Response> cf = new CompletableFuture<>();
asyncHttp.send(req, new Callback() {
    public void onSuccess(Response r) { cf.complete(r); }
    public void onError(Throwable t)  { cf.completeExceptionally(t); }
});
return cf;

Cancellation is weak: cf.cancel(true) completes the future with CancellationException, but it does not interrupt the thread running the supplier — the work continues in the background. If real cancellation matters, check a flag in the task, use timeouts on the underlying calls, or use structured concurrency (StructuredTaskScope), which cancels sibling subtasks on failure.

Pitfalls checklist

Pitfall the default async pool is ForkJoinPool.commonPool(), sized to cores − 1 and shared with parallel streams and other libraries. Blocking I/O there starves the whole JVM. Pass your own executor (or a virtual-thread executor) for I/O.

  • Forgetting a timeout: one hung dependency hangs the whole chain. Use orTimeout and timeouts on the HTTP client.
  • Calling join()/get() inside a stage running on a small pool: thread-starvation deadlock.
  • Losing context: MDC, security context and tracing don't propagate automatically to async stages; wrap the executor (Spring TaskDecorator, Micrometer context propagation).
  • exceptionally placed too early recovers only the failures above it; failures after it propagate.

CompletableFuture vs virtual threads: with JDK 21, simple fan-out can also be written as straightforward blocking code in virtual threads (executor.invokeAll or StructuredTaskScope), which is easier to read and debug. CF remains the tool for composing results from APIs that are already asynchronous.

concurrency-synchronizers-overview.tldr:
• Semaphore limits concurrency; CountDownLatch waits for N events once; CyclicBarrier makes N threads meet repeatedly; Phaser does dynamic phases.
  • BlockingQueue is the producer–consumer tool; CompletableFuture composes async results without blocking.
  • Use a lock, not a semaphore, to protect shared state.
  • Pick by asking: limit, wait-once, meet-repeatedly, hand-off, or compose?
concurrency-synchronizers-overview.body:
Synchronizers are objects that coordinate the control flow of threads based on state: "wait until N things happened", "only K threads at a time", "everyone meet here before continuing", "hand items from producers to consumers". They live in java.util.concurrent and almost all of them are built on one framework, AbstractQueuedSynchronizer (AQS).

The one-line mental model for each

Synchronizer Mental model Question it answers
Semaphore a bowl of N tokens "may I proceed? only N at a time"
CountDownLatch a gate that opens once a counter hits zero "have all N events happened yet?"
CyclicBarrier a meeting point for N parties, reusable "has everyone arrived so we can all continue?"
Phaser a reusable barrier with dynamic membership and numbered phases "multi-phase work where parties come and go"
Exchanger a two-thread swap point "trade my buffer for yours"
BlockingQueue a bounded conveyor belt "pass work from producers to consumers safely"
Lock + Condition a mutex with named waiting rooms "custom wait-until-predicate logic"
CompletableFuture a promise of one result "do this when that async result is ready"

Decision guide

You need to… Use
Limit concurrent access to a resource (DB connections, API calls, licences) Semaphore(n)
Make one or more threads wait until N other operations finish, once CountDownLatch(n)
Release many threads at the same instant (start gate) CountDownLatch(1)
Run rounds where N threads must all finish round k before round k+1 CyclicBarrier(n)
Rounds with a changing number of participants, or a tree of tasks Phaser
Pass items between threads with backpressure BlockingQueue (producer–consumer)
Combine async results without blocking threads CompletableFuture.allOf / thenCombine
Mutual exclusion on shared state synchronized / ReentrantLock (not a semaphore)

The following guides cover each one in depth: how it works inside, its full API, real use cases, runnable programs, the pitfalls that cause production hangs, and the interview questions around it.

concurrency-aqs.tldr:
• AQS = a volatile state changed by CAS + a FIFO queue of parked threads + template methods.
  • Exclusive mode backs locks; shared mode backs Semaphore, CountDownLatch and read locks.
  • state means hold count, permits or remaining count depending on the synchronizer.
  • Non-fair modes let arriving threads barge for throughput; fair modes serve strictly FIFO.

concurrency-semaphore.tldr:
• Permits have no owner: any thread may release, which enables signalling but makes leaks and over-release easy.
  • Acquire first, then try { … } finally { release(); } — never acquire inside the try.
  • Prefer tryAcquire(timeout) for bulkheads so overload becomes a fast rejection, not a hang.
  • With virtual threads, a Semaphore is the standard way to cap pressure on databases and APIs.

concurrency-countdownlatch.tldr:
• One-shot gate: waiters block until countDown() brings the count to zero; it can't be reset.
  • countDown() happens-before a successful await() return, so workers' results are visible.
  • Always count down in finally and await with a timeout, or one failed worker hangs the caller forever.
  • CountDownLatch(1) is a start gate that releases many threads at once.

concurrency-cyclicbarrier.tldr:
• N parties wait for each other; the last arrival runs the barrier action, then all proceed and the barrier resets.
  • Interrupt, timeout or an action exception breaks the barrier: everyone gets BrokenBarrierException; recover with reset().
  • A pool with fewer threads than parties deadlocks.
  • Latch = wait for events signalled by others; barrier = wait for each other, repeatedly.

concurrency-phaser.tldr:
• Phaser is a reusable barrier with numbered phases where parties can register and deregister at runtime.
  • arriveAndAwaitAdvance waits; arrive doesn't; onAdvance can terminate the phaser.
  • Exchanger swaps objects between exactly two threads, e.g. double buffering.
  • Tiered phasers reduce contention with thousands of parties.

concurrency-producerconsumer.tldr:
• A bounded buffer gives backpressure: producers block when full, consumers block when empty.
  • By hand: while-guarded wait/notifyAll, or a lock with notFull/notEmpty conditions; in production: a bounded BlockingQueue.
  • Stop consumers with one poison pill per consumer after producers finish, or by interruption.
  • Never use an unbounded queue; never do slow I/O while holding the buffer's lock.
concurrency-producerconsumer.body:
The problem: producers create work items and consumers process them, at different and varying speeds. A shared bounded buffer sits between them. The rules:

  1. Producers block (or back off) when the buffer is full — this is backpressure.
  2. Consumers block when the buffer is empty — no busy-waiting.
  3. The buffer must be thread-safe with many producers and many consumers.
  4. There must be a clean shutdown: consumers finish remaining work and stop.

It's everywhere in real systems: ThreadPoolExecutor (submitters produce tasks into the work queue, workers consume), async log appenders, Kafka (producers → partitions → consumer groups), request buffering in servers, batch writers to databases.

There are four classic implementations. Interviewers often ask for #1 or #2 by hand, then ask what you'd use in production (#4).

Implementation 1 — synchronized + wait() / notifyAll()

Java
import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Queue;

public class WaitNotifyBuffer<T> {
    private final Queue<T> queue = new ArrayDeque<>();
    private final int capacity;
    public WaitNotifyBuffer(int capacity) { this.capacity = capacity; }

    public synchronized void put(T item) throws InterruptedException {
        while (queue.size() == capacity) wait();     // WHILE: spurious wakeups + another producer may fill it first
        queue.add(item);
        notifyAll();                                 // ALL: notify() could wake another producer and stall consumers
    }

    public synchronized T take() throws InterruptedException {
        while (queue.isEmpty()) wait();
        T item = queue.poll();
        notifyAll();
        return item;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        WaitNotifyBuffer<Integer> buf = new WaitNotifyBuffer<>(2);
        Thread producer = new Thread(() -> {
            try { for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) { buf.put(i); System.out.println("produced " + i); } }
            catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }
        });
        Thread consumer = new Thread(() -> {
            try { for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) { Thread.sleep(100); System.out.println("  consumed " + buf.take()); } }
            catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }
        });
        producer.start(); consumer.start(); producer.join(); consumer.join();
    }
}

Why while and not if: after waking, the condition may no longer hold (another consumer took the item first, or the wakeup was spurious). Why notifyAll and not notify: producers and consumers share one wait-set; notify() might wake a thread of the wrong kind, which goes back to waiting, and everyone stalls.

Implementation 2 — ReentrantLock + two Conditions (targeted wakeups)

Java
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.*;

public class ConditionBuffer<T> {
    private final Object[] items;
    private int putIdx, takeIdx, count;
    private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();
    private final Condition notFull = lock.newCondition();
    private final Condition notEmpty = lock.newCondition();

    public ConditionBuffer(int capacity) { items = new Object[capacity]; }

    public void put(T item) throws InterruptedException {
        lock.lockInterruptibly();
        try {
            while (count == items.length) notFull.await();
            items[putIdx] = item;
            putIdx = (putIdx + 1) % items.length;
            count++;
            notEmpty.signal();                       // wake exactly one CONSUMER
        } finally { lock.unlock(); }
    }

    /** Timed offer: gives up instead of blocking forever (lets callers apply their own backpressure policy). */
    public boolean offer(T item, long timeout, TimeUnit unit) throws InterruptedException {
        long nanos = unit.toNanos(timeout);
        lock.lockInterruptibly();
        try {
            while (count == items.length) {
                if (nanos <= 0) return false;
                nanos = notFull.awaitNanos(nanos);
            }
            items[putIdx] = item; putIdx = (putIdx + 1) % items.length; count++;
            notEmpty.signal();
            return true;
        } finally { lock.unlock(); }
    }

    @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
    public T take() throws InterruptedException {
        lock.lockInterruptibly();
        try {
            while (count == 0) notEmpty.await();
            T item = (T) items[takeIdx];
            items[takeIdx] = null;                   // help GC
            takeIdx = (takeIdx + 1) % items.length;
            count--;
            notFull.signal();                        // wake exactly one PRODUCER
            return item;
        } finally { lock.unlock(); }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        ConditionBuffer<String> buf = new ConditionBuffer<>(1);
        buf.put("first");
        System.out.println("offer when full -> " + buf.offer("second", 100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS));  // false
        System.out.println("take -> " + buf.take());
        System.out.println("offer after take -> " + buf.offer("second", 100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)); // true
    }
}

This is essentially how ArrayBlockingQueue is written. Two conditions mean a producer only wakes consumers and vice versa, so signal() (not signalAll()) is safe and cheaper.

Implementation 3 — Semaphores (Dijkstra's classic solution): two counting semaphores track free slots and filled slots; a mutex protects the buffer itself.

Java
import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Queue;
import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore;

public class SemaphoreBuffer<T> {
    private final Queue<T> queue = new ArrayDeque<>();
    private final Semaphore emptySlots;                  // starts at capacity
    private final Semaphore filledSlots = new Semaphore(0);
    private final Object mutex = new Object();

    public SemaphoreBuffer(int capacity) { emptySlots = new Semaphore(capacity); }

    public void put(T item) throws InterruptedException {
        emptySlots.acquire();                            // wait for a free slot (BEFORE taking the mutex)
        synchronized (mutex) { queue.add(item); }
        filledSlots.release();                           // one more item for consumers
    }

    public T take() throws InterruptedException {
        filledSlots.acquire();                           // wait for an item
        T item;
        synchronized (mutex) { item = queue.poll(); }
        emptySlots.release();                            // one more free slot for producers
        return item;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        SemaphoreBuffer<Integer> buf = new SemaphoreBuffer<>(3);
        Thread c = new Thread(() -> {
            try { for (int i = 0; i < 6; i++) System.out.println("consumed " + buf.take()); }
            catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }
        });
        c.start();
        for (int i = 1; i <= 6; i++) buf.put(i);
        c.join();
    }
}

Pitfall acquiring the mutex before emptySlots.acquire() deadlocks: a producer holds the mutex while waiting for a free slot, and the consumer that would free one can't get the mutex. Always wait on the counting semaphore first, then lock.

Implementation 4 — BlockingQueue (what you use in production). Multiple producers and consumers on an executor, a poison pill per consumer for shutdown, and results gathered safely:

Java
import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.*;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

public class OrderPipeline {
    record Order(int id, String customer) {}
    private static final Order POISON = new Order(-1, "__STOP__");    // sentinel compared by identity

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        int producers = 2, consumers = 3, ordersPerProducer = 10;
        BlockingQueue<Order> queue = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(5);      // bounded: producers block when full
        AtomicInteger processed = new AtomicInteger();
        CountDownLatch producersDone = new CountDownLatch(producers);
        ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(producers + consumers);

        for (int p = 0; p < producers; p++) {
            int pid = p;
            pool.submit(() -> {
                try {
                    for (int i = 0; i < ordersPerProducer; i++) {
                        queue.put(new Order(pid * 100 + i, "cust-" + i));   // blocks when full = backpressure
                    }
                } catch (InterruptedException e) {
                    Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
                } finally {
                    producersDone.countDown();
                }
            });
        }

        for (int c = 0; c < consumers; c++) {
            int cid = c;
            pool.submit(() -> {
                try {
                    while (true) {
                        Order o = queue.take();                  // blocks when empty
                        if (o == POISON) break;                  // shutdown signal
                        Thread.sleep(20);                        // simulated processing
                        processed.incrementAndGet();
                    }
                    System.out.println("consumer " + cid + " stopped");
                } catch (InterruptedException e) {
                    Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
                }
            });
        }

        producersDone.await();                                   // all real work is enqueued
        for (int c = 0; c < consumers; c++) queue.put(POISON);   // ONE pill per consumer, after the real items
        pool.shutdown();
        pool.awaitTermination(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
        System.out.println("processed " + processed.get() + " of " + producers * ordersPerProducer);
    }
}

Because BlockingQueue is FIFO and the pills go in after every real item, each consumer only sees its pill once the real work ahead of it is drained.

Shutdown strategies compared

Strategy How Pros Cons
Poison pill enqueue N sentinels for N consumers drains all queued work; simple must know consumer count; producers must finish first
Interrupt executor.shutdownNow() immediate in-flight and queued items are dropped (returned by shutdownNow)
Flag + timed poll while (running || !q.isEmpty()) { item = q.poll(100, ms); … } no sentinel type needed polling latency; flag must be volatile
Closeable queue wrap the queue with a closed state that makes take return empty cleanest API write it yourself

Batching consumer — drain many items per wake-up (fewer DB round trips):

Java
import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class BatchingConsumer {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        BlockingQueue<String> q = new LinkedBlockingQueue<>(10_000);
        for (int i = 0; i < 250; i++) q.put("event-" + i);

        List<String> batch = new ArrayList<>(100);
        int batches = 0;
        while (!q.isEmpty()) {
            String first = q.poll(500, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);   // wait for at least one item
            if (first == null) continue;
            batch.add(first);
            q.drainTo(batch, 99);                                // grab up to 99 more without blocking
            batches++;
            System.out.println("bulk insert of " + batch.size() + " rows");
            batch.clear();
        }
        System.out.println(batches + " batches");
    }
}

Choosing the queue

Queue Bounded Notes Use when
ArrayBlockingQueue yes (fixed) one lock for put and take, array backed, optional fairness default bounded buffer, predictable memory
LinkedBlockingQueue optional (default Integer.MAX_VALUE!) separate put/take locks → higher throughput with both sides busy high throughput; always pass a capacity
SynchronousQueue capacity 0 each put waits for a take (direct hand-off) newCachedThreadPool; no buffering wanted
PriorityBlockingQueue unbounded ordered by comparator priority jobs (add your own bound)
DelayQueue unbounded items available after their delay scheduled retries, TTL expiry
LinkedTransferQueue unbounded transfer() waits until consumed hand-off with optional buffering
ArrayDeque (not thread-safe) — — single-thread only
LMAX Disruptor (library) ring buffer lock-free, pre-allocated, mechanical sympathy ultra-low-latency pipelines

Backpressure policies when the buffer is full

Policy API Effect
Block the producer put() producers slow to the consumers' pace (default choice)
Block with timeout, then fail offer(e, timeout, unit) bounded wait, caller handles rejection
Reject immediately offer(e) returns false shed load, return 429/503
Drop oldest poll() then offer() keep freshest data (metrics, telemetry)
Run in caller ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy the producer does the work itself

Pitfalls checklist

Pitfall an unbounded queue (new LinkedBlockingQueue<>() with no capacity, or Executors.newFixedThreadPool) removes backpressure entirely. When consumers fall behind, memory grows until OutOfMemoryError. Always bound the buffer.

  • if instead of while around wait()/await() — breaks with multiple consumers and spurious wakeups.
  • notify() with mixed producers and consumers on one monitor — lost wakeups and stalls.
  • Calling wait() without holding the monitor → IllegalMonitorStateException.
  • Swallowing InterruptedException in consumers → they can never be stopped.
  • Fewer poison pills than consumers → some consumers block forever; pills sent before producers finish → consumers stop early.
  • Doing slow work (I/O) while holding the buffer's lock — take the item, release, then process.
  • Mutable items shared after put() — the producer must not modify an item once handed off.

Producer–consumer with virtual threads: the code above works unchanged with Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(). BlockingQueue uses ReentrantLock, so blocking in put/take unmounts the virtual thread instead of pinning a carrier.

concurrency-synchronizers-qa.tldr:
• You can build a semaphore from a lock + condition, a latch from synchronized + wait/notifyAll, and a barrier with a generation counter.
  • Semaphores aren't reentrant; latches can't reset; barrier actions run in the last arriving thread.
  • Fair semaphores prevent starvation of large acquire(n) requests at a throughput cost.
  • A generation counter stops a fast thread from slipping through the next barrier round.
concurrency-synchronizers-qa.body:
Implement a counting semaphore yourself (a frequent follow-up):

Java
import java.util.concurrent.locks.*;

public class MySemaphore {
    private int permits;
    private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();
    private final Condition available = lock.newCondition();

    public MySemaphore(int permits) { this.permits = permits; }

    public void acquire() throws InterruptedException {
        lock.lockInterruptibly();
        try {
            while (permits == 0) available.await();
            permits--;
        } finally { lock.unlock(); }
    }

    public boolean tryAcquire() {
        lock.lock();
        try { if (permits > 0) { permits--; return true; } return false; }
        finally { lock.unlock(); }
    }

    public void release() {
        lock.lock();
        try { permits++; available.signal(); }
        finally { lock.unlock(); }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        MySemaphore s = new MySemaphore(1);
        s.acquire();
        System.out.println("tryAcquire while held: " + s.tryAcquire());   // false
        s.release();
        System.out.println("tryAcquire after release: " + s.tryAcquire()); // true
    }
}

Implement a CountDownLatch yourself

Java
public class MyCountDownLatch {
    private int count;
    public MyCountDownLatch(int count) {
        if (count < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("count < 0");
        this.count = count;
    }
    public synchronized void countDown() {
        if (count > 0 && --count == 0) notifyAll();       // open the gate for every waiter
    }
    public synchronized void await() throws InterruptedException {
        while (count > 0) wait();
    }
    public synchronized long getCount() { return count; }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        MyCountDownLatch latch = new MyCountDownLatch(3);
        for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) new Thread(latch::countDown).start();
        latch.await();
        System.out.println("all three counted down, count=" + latch.getCount());
    }
}

Implement a reusable CyclicBarrier yourself (generation counter prevents a fast thread from slipping through the next round):

Java
public class MyCyclicBarrier {
    private final int parties;
    private int waiting;
    private long generation;
    private final Runnable action;

    public MyCyclicBarrier(int parties, Runnable action) { this.parties = parties; this.action = action; }

    public synchronized void await() throws InterruptedException {
        long myGen = generation;
        if (++waiting == parties) {                      // last to arrive
            if (action != null) action.run();
            waiting = 0;
            generation++;                                // start the next round
            notifyAll();
            return;
        }
        while (myGen == generation) wait();              // wait until THIS round trips
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        MyCyclicBarrier b = new MyCyclicBarrier(3, () -> System.out.println("-- trip --"));
        Runnable r = () -> {
            try { for (int i = 0; i < 2; i++) b.await(); } catch (InterruptedException ignored) { }
        };
        Thread[] ts = { new Thread(r), new Thread(r), new Thread(r) };
        for (Thread t : ts) t.start();
        for (Thread t : ts) t.join();
    }
}

Quick answers

Question Answer
Can a thread release a Semaphore permit it never acquired? Yes — no ownership; it increases the permit count.
Is Semaphore reentrant? No. Acquiring twice with one permit self-deadlocks.
Can CountDownLatch be reset? No. Create a new one, or use CyclicBarrier/Phaser.
What does countDown() do at zero? Nothing; it stays at zero.
Which thread runs the CyclicBarrier action? The last thread to arrive, before any party is released.
What if one party is interrupted at a barrier? The barrier breaks; all waiting parties get BrokenBarrierException.
await() return value of CyclicBarrier? Arrival index: parties - 1 for the first arrival, 0 for the last.
Can the latch count differ from the number of threads? Yes — it counts events, not threads.
Fair Semaphore: why and cost? FIFO order prevents starvation of large acquire(n) requests; lower throughput.
Why bounded queues in producer–consumer? Backpressure; unbounded queues hide overload until OOM.

concurrency-collections.tldr:
• ConcurrentHashMap: CAS into empty bins, lock only the bin head, lock-free reads, cooperative resize, no nulls.
  • Use atomic per-key operations (merge, compute, computeIfAbsent) instead of get-then-put.
  • CopyOnWriteArrayList suits read-mostly listener lists; iterators never throw CME.
  • Know the BlockingQueue methods: put/take block, offer/poll return special values, timed variants wait.
concurrency-collections.body:
Wrapping a collection with Collections.synchronizedXxx makes every method lock one global mutex: correct but slow under contention, and you still need manual locking for iteration and compound actions. The java.util.concurrent collections are designed for concurrency from the inside.

Choosing a collection

Need Use Avoid
Thread-safe map ConcurrentHashMap Hashtable, Collections.synchronizedMap (one global lock)
Sorted concurrent map/set ConcurrentSkipListMap / ConcurrentSkipListSet synchronized TreeMap
Read-mostly list (listeners, config) CopyOnWriteArrayList for write-heavy lists
Producer/consumer queue ArrayBlockingQueue, LinkedBlockingQueue (bounded) hand-written wait/notify
Non-blocking FIFO ConcurrentLinkedQueue / ConcurrentLinkedDeque
Direct hand-off, no buffer SynchronousQueue
Delayed / scheduled items DelayQueue
Priority order PriorityBlockingQueue (unbounded — add your own bound)
Concurrent set ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet() Collections.synchronizedSet

ConcurrentHashMap (Java 8+) — the structure

How put works

Key implementation facts:

  • Reads take no lock: get reads volatile table slots and node fields, so it sees the latest completed write.
  • Writes lock one bin, not the whole map; threads writing different bins never contend. (Java 7 used 16 ReentrantLock "segments" by default instead; interviewers still ask about it.)
  • Treeification: a bin with ≥ 8 nodes (when the table has ≥ 64 slots) becomes a red-black tree, so worst-case lookup is O(log n) even with bad hash codes.
  • Cooperative resizing: when a resize is in progress, threads that touch the map help move bins to the new table; moved bins hold a ForwardingNode.
  • size() sums baseCount and striped counter cells (like LongAdder), so it's fast but only an estimate while writers are active. mappingCount() returns a long.
  • No null keys or values: get returning null must unambiguously mean "absent"; with nulls you couldn't tell "absent" from "mapped to null" without a racy second call.
  • Weakly consistent iterators: they never throw ConcurrentModificationException; they reflect the map at some point at or after creation and may or may not show later updates.

Atomic compound operations — the part that matters most in real code

Java
ConcurrentHashMap<String, Integer> counts = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

// WRONG: check-then-act race between get and put (two threads both read null, both write 1)
Integer c = counts.get(word);
counts.put(word, c == null ? 1 : c + 1);

// RIGHT: each of these is atomic for that key
counts.merge(word, 1, Integer::sum);
counts.compute(word, (k, v) -> v == null ? 1 : v + 1);
counts.putIfAbsent(word, 0);

// Lazy per-key initialization: the function runs at most once per key
Map<String, Connection> conns = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
Connection conn = conns.computeIfAbsent(host, h -> connect(h));

// High-contention counters: one LongAdder per key
ConcurrentHashMap<String, LongAdder> freq = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
freq.computeIfAbsent(word, k -> new LongAdder()).increment();

Pitfall the remapping function in compute/computeIfAbsent/merge runs while holding the bin lock. Keep it short, never block or do I/O in it, and never modify the same map from inside it (that can deadlock or throw IllegalStateException: Recursive update).

Bulk operations (forEach, search, reduce with a parallelismThreshold) run in parallel on the common pool for large maps:

Java
long total = prices.reduceValuesToLong(10_000, Long::longValue, 0L, Long::sum);
String firstExpensive = prices.search(10_000, (k, v) -> v > 1_000 ? k : null);

CopyOnWriteArrayList — every write copies the whole backing array; readers and iterators work on an immutable snapshot, so iteration needs no locking and never throws CME. Perfect for listener lists (rare writes, frequent iteration); terrible for lists with frequent writes (O(n) copy per write).

ConcurrentSkipListMap — a lock-free sorted map built on a skip list: a sorted linked list with extra "express lanes" of index levels, giving O(log n) operations without tree rebalancing locks.

Use it for concurrent ordered data: leaderboards in memory, time-ordered buffers, range queries (subMap, headMap, ceilingKey).

BlockingQueue method families

Throws exception Returns special value Blocks Times out
Insert add(e) offer(e) → false put(e) offer(e, t, unit)
Remove remove() poll() → null take() poll(t, unit)
Examine element() peek() → null — —

ArrayBlockingQueue uses one lock for both ends; LinkedBlockingQueue uses separate put and take locks (higher throughput when producers and consumers are both busy) but allocates a node per element and is unbounded by default — always pass a capacity.

concurrency-forkjoin.tldr:
• Work stealing: each worker has a deque; idle workers steal old, large tasks from others' tails.
  • Fork one half, compute the other, then join; choose a sensible sequential threshold.
  • Parallel streams run on the shared common pool: use them only for large, CPU-bound, splittable work.
  • Avoid parallel streams with blocking I/O, LinkedList sources or shared mutable state.
concurrency-forkjoin.body:
ForkJoinPool is built for divide-and-conquer: split a big task into subtasks recursively until they're small, solve those directly, and combine the results.

Work stealing. Each worker thread owns a deque of tasks. A worker pushes the subtasks it forks onto the head of its own deque and pops from the head (LIFO: the most recent, cache-warm, smallest tasks). An idle worker steals from the tail of another worker's deque (FIFO: the oldest, biggest tasks), so a single steal gets a large chunk of work and contention between owner and thief is rare.

Java
class SumTask extends RecursiveTask<Long> {
    private static final int THRESHOLD = 10_000;
    private final long[] arr; private final int lo, hi;
    SumTask(long[] arr, int lo, int hi) { this.arr = arr; this.lo = lo; this.hi = hi; }

    @Override protected Long compute() {
        if (hi - lo <= THRESHOLD) {
            long s = 0;
            for (int i = lo; i < hi; i++) s += arr[i];
            return s;
        }
        int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;
        SumTask left = new SumTask(arr, lo, mid);
        SumTask right = new SumTask(arr, mid, hi);
        left.fork();                       // push to own deque (may be stolen)
        long r = right.compute();          // do the other half in this thread
        return r + left.join();            // join: if not stolen, run it here; else help others while waiting
    }
}
long total = ForkJoinPool.commonPool().invoke(new SumTask(data, 0, data.length));

Rules: fork one half and compute the other in the current thread (forking both wastes this thread); pick a threshold so leaf tasks take roughly 10–100 µs (too small = overhead dominates, too large = poor balance); RecursiveAction is the no-result variant; invokeAll(t1, t2) forks and joins a set.

The common pool

  • ForkJoinPool.commonPool() has availableProcessors() − 1 threads by default (configure with -Djava.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool.common.parallelism=N).
  • It's shared: parallel streams, CompletableFuture.*Async without an executor, and some libraries all use it. One component doing blocking I/O there degrades all the others.
  • If you must block inside a ForkJoin task, wrap it in a ForkJoinPool.ManagedBlocker so the pool can add compensating threads.

Parallel streams split the source with its Spliterator, run chunks on the common pool and combine.

Java
long primes = IntStream.rangeClosed(2, 5_000_000).parallel().filter(this::isPrime).count();

// Run a parallel stream on a dedicated pool so it can't starve the common pool
ForkJoinPool custom = new ForkJoinPool(4);
try {
    long result = custom.submit(() -> list.parallelStream().mapToLong(this::score).sum()).get();
} finally {
    custom.shutdown();
}

When does parallel() actually help? A useful rule of thumb is N × Q > 10,000, where N is the number of elements and Q the cost per element (in simple operations). Summing 1,000 integers: not worth it. Scoring 100,000 documents with an expensive function: worth it.

Helps Hurts
large data, expensive per-element work small data, cheap operations (sum of a short list)
sources that split well: arrays, ArrayList, IntStream.range, HashMap LinkedList, Stream.iterate, I/O-backed streams
stateless, non-interfering lambdas shared mutable state (list.add inside forEach), synchronized blocks
associative reductions (sum, max, collectors) order-dependent ops (limit, findFirst on ordered streams), sorted
CPU-bound work blocking I/O (starves the common pool)

Pitfall parallelStream().forEach(results::add) on an ArrayList loses elements or throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException. Use collect(...)/toList(), which merges per-thread partial results safely.

concurrency-threadlocal.tldr:
• Each thread gets its own copy; values live in the thread's map, so pooled threads keep them forever.
  • Always remove() in finally, or you leak memory and leak data between requests.
  • InheritableThreadLocal goes stale with pools; propagate context explicitly (TaskDecorator, context propagation).
  • ScopedValue (final in JDK 25) is the immutable, bounded, virtual-thread-friendly replacement.
concurrency-threadlocal.body:
ThreadLocal<T> gives each thread its own independent copy of a variable. Common uses: per-request context (user id, tenant, trace id — SLF4J's MDC is a ThreadLocal), transaction context (Spring's TransactionSynchronizationManager, security context SecurityContextHolder), and per-thread instances of non-thread-safe helpers (SimpleDateFormat, Cipher, MessageDigest).

Where the values actually live

Each Thread holds a ThreadLocalMap; the ThreadLocal object is only the key. get() looks up the current thread's map with this as the key. Keys are weak references (so an unreachable ThreadLocal can be collected), but values are strong references.

Java
public final class RequestContext {
    private static final ThreadLocal<String> USER = new ThreadLocal<>();
    public static void set(String u) { USER.set(u); }
    public static String get() { return USER.get(); }
    public static void clear() { USER.remove(); }
}

// In a servlet filter: set at the start, ALWAYS clear at the end
@Component
public class UserContextFilter extends OncePerRequestFilter {
    @Override
    protected void doFilterInternal(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse res, FilterChain chain)
            throws ServletException, IOException {
        try {
            RequestContext.set(extractUser(req));
            chain.doFilter(req, res);
        } finally {
            RequestContext.clear();            // CRITICAL with pooled threads
        }
    }
}

Why it leaks

Two failure modes from forgetting remove() on pool threads, which live as long as the application:

  1. Data leak between requests (the next request on that thread sees the previous user's context) — a security bug.
  2. Memory leak: big values (caches, buffers) stay reachable from the thread forever. In application servers, a value whose class came from a web app's classloader pins the whole classloader after redeploy (Metaspace leak).

Propagating context to other threads. ThreadLocals don't cross thread boundaries. InheritableThreadLocal copies values when a child thread is created, which is useless with pools (threads are created once, so values go stale). Propagate explicitly:

Java
// Spring: copy MDC (and similarly SecurityContext) into @Async / executor tasks
public class MdcTaskDecorator implements TaskDecorator {
    @Override public Runnable decorate(Runnable task) {
        Map<String, String> context = MDC.getCopyOfContextMap();       // captured on the submitting thread
        return () -> {
            Map<String, String> previous = MDC.getCopyOfContextMap();
            try {
                if (context != null) MDC.setContextMap(context); else MDC.clear();
                task.run();
            } finally {
                if (previous != null) MDC.setContextMap(previous); else MDC.clear();   // restore the worker's state
            }
        };
    }
}
// executor.setTaskDecorator(new MdcTaskDecorator());
// Spring Boot 3 + Micrometer: ContextPropagatingTaskDecorator propagates observation/tracing context too.

ThreadLocal and virtual threads. ThreadLocals work with virtual threads, but there can be millions of virtual threads, so a per-thread cache (e.g. a 1 MB buffer per thread) multiplies into gigabytes. Don't use ThreadLocals as object pools with virtual threads.

ScopedValue (preview in JDK 21–24, final in JDK 25) is the modern replacement for request-scoped context: an immutable value bound for the duration of a method call, automatically unbound afterwards, cheaply inherited by child threads in structured concurrency.

Java
static final ScopedValue<String> USER = ScopedValue.newInstance();

void handle(Request req) {
    ScopedValue.where(USER, req.user()).run(() -> service.process(req));   // bound only inside run()
}
// anywhere below in the call stack: USER.get()  -> the bound value; outside: NoSuchElementException
ThreadLocal ScopedValue
Mutability set() anywhere immutable for the scope
Lifetime until remove() or the thread dies exactly the run()/call() scope
Leak risk high with pools none by design
Inheritance InheritableThreadLocal copies (expensive) shared cheaply with StructuredTaskScope children

concurrency-virtualthreads.tldr:
• Virtual threads unmount from carrier threads when they block, making thread-per-request scale to millions.
  • They speed up blocking I/O, not CPU-bound work; don't pool them.
  • Bound downstream resources explicitly (Semaphore, connection pool size).
  • Pinning inside synchronized was fixed in JDK 24; on 21–23 prefer ReentrantLock around blocking calls.

concurrency-liveness.tldr:
• Deadlock needs mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption and circular wait; break one (usually lock ordering).
  • tryLock with timeout and random back-off avoids both deadlock and livelock.
  • Diagnose with several thread dumps (jcmd <pid> Thread.print) and ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads().
  • Watch for thread-starvation deadlock: tasks blocking on subtasks queued in the same bounded pool.
concurrency-liveness.body:
Liveness means the program keeps making progress. The three classic failures:

Failure What happens Example
Deadlock threads wait for each other forever; nobody runs T1 holds A wants B, T2 holds B wants A
Livelock threads keep running and reacting to each other but make no progress two transfers that both back off and retry in lockstep
Starvation a thread never gets the resource it needs an unfair lock or a constant stream of readers starving a writer

Deadlock as a cycle in the wait-for graph

A deadlock requires all four Coffman conditions; breaking any one prevents it:

Condition Meaning How to break it
Mutual exclusion a resource is held by one thread at a time lock-free structures, immutable data
Hold and wait a thread holds one lock while waiting for another acquire all locks at once, or tryLock and release on failure
No preemption locks can't be taken away timeouts (tryLock(timeout)) so threads give up
Circular wait a cycle of waiting threads global lock ordering (most common fix)
Java
// Deadlock: transfer(a, b) and transfer(b, a) concurrently
void transfer(Account from, Account to, long amt) {
    synchronized (from) {
        synchronized (to) { from.debit(amt); to.credit(amt); }
    }
}

// Fix 1: global lock ordering (breaks circular wait)
void transferSafe(Account from, Account to, long amt) {
    Account first  = from.id() < to.id() ? from : to;
    Account second = from.id() < to.id() ? to : from;
    synchronized (first) {
        synchronized (second) { from.debit(amt); to.credit(amt); }
    }
}

// Fix 2: tryLock with timeout and random back-off (breaks hold-and-wait; avoids livelock)
boolean tryTransfer(Account from, Account to, long amt) throws InterruptedException {
    while (true) {
        if (from.lock.tryLock(50, MILLISECONDS)) {
            try {
                if (to.lock.tryLock(50, MILLISECONDS)) {
                    try { from.debit(amt); to.credit(amt); return true; }
                    finally { to.lock.unlock(); }
                }
            } finally { from.lock.unlock(); }
        }
        Thread.sleep(ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextInt(1, 10));   // random back-off breaks lockstep retries
    }
}

Livelock usually comes from symmetric retry logic: both threads detect the conflict at the same moment, both back off the same amount, both retry together. Randomized back-off (with jitter) fixes it — the same reason network protocols use random exponential back-off.

Starvation comes from unfair scheduling: non-fair locks where one thread keeps re-acquiring, read-write locks with constant readers, a thread pool where long tasks starve short ones, or thread priorities. Fixes: fair locks where it matters, bounded time holding a lock, separate pools for different workloads.

Priority inversion: a low-priority thread holds a lock a high-priority thread needs, while medium-priority threads keep the low one from running. Rare in Java services (priorities are mostly ignored), but worth naming.

Deadlocks that aren't about locks

  • Thread-starvation deadlock: a task in a bounded pool submits a subtask to the same pool and blocks on get(); when every worker does this, all wait for subtasks that can never run.
  • A CountDownLatch never counted down (exception before countDown()), a CyclicBarrier with fewer threads than parties, a semaphore permit leak.
  • Database deadlocks and lock waits (see Databases → MVCC and locks).

Finding them in production

Shell
jcmd <pid> Thread.print > dump.txt     # or: jstack -l <pid>  (-l adds owned java.util.concurrent locks)
# The JVM detects monitor and j.u.c lock cycles and prints "Found one Java-level deadlock:"
# For other hangs: take 3 dumps 5–10 s apart; threads stuck on the same frame in all of them are the problem.
jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json threads.json   # JDK 21: includes virtual threads
Java
// Programmatic detection, e.g. inside a health indicator or a watchdog thread
ThreadMXBean mx = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean();
long[] ids = mx.findDeadlockedThreads();          // monitors + ownable synchronizers (ReentrantLock etc.)
if (ids != null) {
    for (ThreadInfo ti : mx.getThreadInfo(ids, true, true)) log.error("Deadlocked: {}", ti);
}

Prevention checklist: acquire multiple locks in a global order; never call alien code (callbacks, listeners, overridable methods) while holding a lock; keep critical sections short and free of I/O; prefer tryLock with timeouts and timeouts on every blocking wait (await(t), get(t), poll(t)); use separate executors for tasks that wait on each other; prefer higher-level constructs (concurrent collections, queues, immutable data) over hand-rolled locking.

concurrency-patterns.tldr:
• Immutability is the simplest thread safety: final class, final fields, defensive copies, or records.
  • Lazy singletons: double-checked locking needs volatile; the holder idiom and enums are simpler.
  • Thread confinement (one owner thread) needs no synchronization: event loops, Kafka consumers.
