  • Other patterns: striped locks per key, single-writer, read-copy-update with AtomicReference.
concurrency-patterns.body:
The safest shared state is no shared mutable state. Most concurrency patterns are ways to avoid sharing, avoid mutating, or make the remaining sharing explicit.

1. Immutability — no writes after construction means no races, no locks, free sharing.

Java
public final class Money {                       // final class: no mutable subclasses
    private final BigDecimal amount;             // all fields final and private
    private final Currency currency;
    private final List<String> tags;

    public Money(BigDecimal amount, Currency currency, List<String> tags) {
        this.amount = amount;
        this.currency = currency;
        this.tags = List.copyOf(tags);           // defensive copy in (and unmodifiable)
    }
    public List<String> tags() { return tags; }  // safe to expose
    public Money plus(Money o) {                 // "mutators" return new objects
        return new Money(amount.add(o.amount), currency, tags);
    }
}
// Or simply: public record Money(BigDecimal amount, Currency currency) {} with immutable component types

2. Thread-safe lazy singletons

Java
// a) Double-checked locking: volatile is REQUIRED (without it, another thread may see a half-built object)
public final class Registry {
    private static volatile Registry instance;
    private Registry() {}
    public static Registry getInstance() {
        Registry r = instance;                    // one volatile read on the fast path
        if (r == null) {
            synchronized (Registry.class) {
                r = instance;
                if (r == null) instance = r = new Registry();
            }
        }
        return r;
    }
}

// b) Holder idiom: lazy and lock-free, because class initialization is guaranteed thread-safe by the JVM
public final class Config {
    private Config() {}
    private static class Holder { static final Config INSTANCE = new Config(); }
    public static Config getInstance() { return Holder.INSTANCE; }   // Holder is initialized on first call
}

// c) Enum: also safe against serialization and reflection attacks
public enum Metrics { INSTANCE; public void record(String k) { } }

Why DCL needs volatile: instance = new Registry() is allocate → construct → assign; without volatile the assignment may become visible before the constructor's writes, so a second thread sees a non-null but uninitialized object.

3. Thread confinement — only one thread ever touches the object. Examples: local variables (stack confinement), ThreadLocal, each Kafka consumer thread owning its KafkaConsumer (it's not thread-safe), and event loops (Netty, Node.js, Vert.x).

The actor model (Akka/Pekko) generalizes this: each actor owns its state and processes one message at a time from its mailbox.

4. Single-writer principle — exactly one thread writes a piece of state; others only read it (via volatile/atomics or immutable snapshots). Eliminates write contention entirely; the LMAX Disruptor is built on it.

5. Copy-on-write / read-copy-update — readers read the current immutable snapshot without locks; a writer copies, modifies the copy, and atomically swaps the reference.

Java
private final AtomicReference<Map<String, Route>> routes = new AtomicReference<>(Map.of());

Route lookup(String path) { return routes.get().get(path); }          // lock-free read

void addRoute(String path, Route r) {
    routes.updateAndGet(old -> {
        Map<String, Route> copy = new HashMap<>(old);
        copy.put(path, r);
        return Map.copyOf(copy);                                       // publish a new immutable snapshot
    });
}

6. Striped (per-key) locks — instead of one global lock, hash keys onto N locks so unrelated keys don't contend.

Java
private final ReentrantLock[] stripes = IntStream.range(0, 64).mapToObj(i -> new ReentrantLock()).toArray(ReentrantLock[]::new);
private ReentrantLock lockFor(Object key) { return stripes[Math.floorMod(key.hashCode(), stripes.length)]; }

void updateAccount(String accountId, Consumer<Account> change) {
    ReentrantLock l = lockFor(accountId);
    l.lock();
    try { change.accept(accounts.get(accountId)); } finally { l.unlock(); }
}
// Guava offers Striped.lock(64); ConcurrentHashMap.compute(key, ...) gives per-key atomicity for map entries.

7. Guarded suspension and balking — guarded suspension waits until a condition holds (while (!ready) wait(), Condition.await, BlockingQueue.take); balking returns immediately if the object isn't in the right state ("already started, ignore this start() call"), typically with an AtomicBoolean.compareAndSet(false, true).

Java
private final AtomicBoolean started = new AtomicBoolean();
public void start() {
    if (!started.compareAndSet(false, true)) return;      // balk: someone else already started it
    worker.start();
}

8. Producer–consumer and pipelines — decouple stages with bounded queues so each stage can run on its own threads with backpressure (covered in depth in the Producer–Consumer guide).

concurrency-problems.tldr:
• Odd/even and ABC printing are turn-taking: a shared turn with wait/notifyAll, or semaphores passing a baton.
  • Producer–consumer with a BlockingQueue and poison pill is the production answer.
  • A thread-safe LRU needs an exclusive lock because get reorders a LinkedHashMap.
  • Token bucket: refill tokens by elapsed time under a lock, then take one.

qa.q: What is the difference between a process and a thread?
qa.a: A process has its own address space and resources; threads live inside a process and share its heap, code and open files, but each has its own stack and program counter. Thread creation and context switches are cheaper; communication is easier (shared memory) but requires synchronization. A crash in one thread (uncaught Error like OOM) can bring down the whole process.

qa.q: Runnable vs Callable?
qa.a: Runnable.run() returns nothing and can't throw checked exceptions. Callable.call() returns a value and can throw Exception. Executors accept both via submit(), returning a Future.

qa.q: What does volatile guarantee, and what doesn't it?
qa.a: Visibility (writes go to main memory; reads see the latest write) and ordering (a volatile write HB subsequent reads; no reordering around it). It does not make compound actions atomic: volatile int x; x++ can lose updates. Use it for status flags, double-checked locking and publishing immutable objects.

qa.q: Explain happens-before with an example.
qa.a: HB is the JMM's guarantee that the effects of action A are visible to action B. Example: thread 1 writes data = 42 then writes volatile ready = true; thread 2 reads ready == true then reads data. Program order (data write HB ready write) + the volatile rule (ready write HB ready read) + transitivity ⇒ thread 2 is guaranteed to see 42. Without the volatile, thread 2 might see ready true and data 0.

qa.q: synchronized vs ReentrantLock — when do you pick each?
qa.a: synchronized is simpler, auto-releases, and fine for most cases. Choose ReentrantLock for tryLock with timeout (deadlock avoidance), interruptible lock acquisition, fairness, multiple Conditions, or (on JDK 21–23) to avoid virtual-thread pinning. Always unlock in finally.

qa.q: Why must wait() be called in a loop?
qa.a: Spurious wakeups are allowed by the spec, and by the time a notified thread reacquires the lock another thread may have consumed the condition. Re-checking the predicate in a while loop handles both.

qa.q: Difference between sleep() and wait()?
qa.a: sleep is a static Thread method; it keeps any held locks and resumes after the timeout. wait is an Object method; it must be called while holding the object's monitor, releases that monitor, and resumes after notify/notifyAll/timeout/interrupt.

qa.q: How does ConcurrentHashMap achieve thread safety?
qa.a: Java 8+: CAS to insert into an empty bin; synchronized on the bin's head node for other writes (so contention is per bin); lock-free volatile reads; treeification of long bins; cooperative multi-threaded resizing; a striped counter for size(). Java 7 used 16 lock-striped segments. Null keys/values are forbidden to avoid ambiguity in concurrent get.

qa.q: Why is HashMap unsafe in concurrent code?
qa.a: Concurrent puts can lose entries, corrupt size, and during resize in Java 7 could create a cycle in a bucket's linked list, making get spin at 100% CPU forever. Java 8 fixed the cycle (tail insertion) but data loss and races remain.

qa.q: What happens when a thread pool's queue is full?
qa.a: If current threads < maximumPoolSize, a new non-core thread is created; otherwise the RejectedExecutionHandler runs (default AbortPolicy throws RejectedExecutionException). CallerRunsPolicy makes the submitter run it, which slows producers down (backpressure).

qa.q: Why shouldn't you use Executors.newFixedThreadPool in production?
qa.a: It uses an unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue. Under sustained overload the queue grows until OutOfMemoryError, and latency grows silently. Build a ThreadPoolExecutor with a bounded queue, named threads, a deliberate rejection policy and metrics.

qa.q: How do you size a thread pool?
qa.a: CPU-bound ≈ number of cores (+1). I/O-bound ≈ cores × (1 + wait/compute). Then validate with load tests, watching CPU utilization, queue depth and p99 latency. Also respect downstream limits: 200 threads calling a database with a 20-connection pool just moves the queue.

qa.q: thenApply vs thenCompose?
qa.a: thenApply(fn) maps the result to a value (T → U). thenCompose(fn) is for functions that themselves return a CompletableFuture (T → CF<U>), flattening it instead of producing CF<CF<U>>. Map vs flatMap.

qa.q: How do you handle exceptions in CompletableFuture?
qa.a: exceptionally (recover with a fallback value), handle (receives result or exception, transforms either), whenComplete (side effect such as logging, result unchanged). Exceptions arrive wrapped in CompletionException; unwrap getCause(). Add orTimeout so a hung call doesn't hang the chain.

qa.q: CountDownLatch vs CyclicBarrier?
qa.a: Latch: one-shot; some threads wait for N events which other threads signal; can't be reset. Barrier: N threads wait for each other, reusable for repeated rounds, with an optional barrier action; if one thread is interrupted the barrier breaks for all.

qa.q: What is a race condition? Give a real example.
qa.a: When the correctness depends on the timing of threads. Check-then-act (if (!map.containsKey(k)) map.put(k, v)) and read-modify-write (count++) are the two classic shapes. Example: two requests both read stock = 1 and both sell the last item.

qa.q: What is false sharing?
qa.a: Two independent variables written by different threads sit on the same 64-byte CPU cache line, so each write invalidates the other core's line and they ping-pong. Fix with padding or @jdk.internal.vm.annotation.Contended (needs -XX:-RestrictContended). LongAdder cells are padded for this reason.

qa.q: How would you detect and fix a deadlock in production?
qa.a: Take several thread dumps (jcmd <pid> Thread.print), look for "Found one Java-level deadlock" or threads BLOCKED waiting on each other's locks. Fix with a global lock order, tryLock with timeouts, smaller lock scopes (never call external code or I/O while holding a lock), or replacing locks with concurrent data structures. Add ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads() to a health check.

qa.q: What are virtual threads, and when would you not use them?
qa.a: JVM-scheduled lightweight threads that unmount from their carrier when they block, making thread-per-request scale to millions of concurrent blocking operations. Don't expect gains for CPU-bound work; don't pool them; watch for pinning in synchronized on JDK 21–23 and for oversized ThreadLocals; and bound downstream resources explicitly because they remove the implicit limit that a thread pool provided.

qa.q: What is the ABA problem?
qa.a: A CAS checks that a value is still A, but it may have changed A → B → A in between, so the CAS succeeds on changed state. It bites lock-free structures with node reuse. Fix with AtomicStampedReference (version stamp) or by never reusing nodes (GC helps in Java).

qa.q: Is i++ thread-safe? What about AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet()?
qa.a: i++ is not; it's three steps (read, add, write). incrementAndGet is, via a CAS retry loop. Under very high contention, LongAdder beats both.

qa.q: What's the difference between execute() and submit()?
qa.a: execute(Runnable) returns nothing and lets exceptions reach the thread's uncaught exception handler. submit() returns a Future and stores exceptions inside it; if you never call get(), failures are silently swallowed.

qa.q: How do you propagate MDC / security context to async threads?
qa.a: ThreadLocals don't cross thread boundaries. Wrap tasks: Spring's TaskDecorator on ThreadPoolTaskExecutor copies the MDC map and SecurityContext into the worker and clears them after; DelegatingSecurityContextExecutor; or Micrometer Context Propagation for Reactor and @Async.

qa.q: What is thread-starvation deadlock?
qa.a: A task running in a bounded pool submits a subtask to the same pool and blocks on its result. When all workers do this, every thread waits for subtasks that can never get a thread. Fix: separate pools per stage, non-blocking composition (thenCompose), or ForkJoin's work-stealing join.

qa.q: Semaphore vs mutex (lock) — what's the difference?
qa.a: A mutex/lock has exactly one owner, only the owner can unlock it, and ReentrantLock is reentrant; it protects shared state. A semaphore has N permits, no ownership (any thread can release, even one that never acquired), and isn't reentrant; it limits how many threads do something concurrently or signals between threads. A binary semaphore looks like a lock but lacks ownership and reentrancy.

qa.q: How would you limit an endpoint to 10 concurrent calls to a downstream service?
qa.a: A Semaphore(10) around the call: tryAcquire(timeout) so callers fail fast with a fallback instead of queuing forever, the call in try, release() in finally. In Spring this is Resilience4j's semaphore bulkhead. With virtual threads this is the standard way to bound pressure on a database or API.

qa.q: What happens if a worker throws before calling countDown()?
qa.a: The count never reaches zero and every await() blocks forever, which shows up as threads parked in CountDownLatch.await in a thread dump. Always call countDown() in finally, and await with a timeout so a missing event becomes a handled failure rather than a hang.

qa.q: When would you use CountDownLatch(1)?
qa.a: As a start gate: many threads await() on it and the coordinator calls countDown() once to release them all at the same instant. Used in load/concurrency tests and to make workers start only after setup completes. It's also the simplest one-shot "signal received" flag for tests of async callbacks.

qa.q: What happens to a CyclicBarrier if one thread is interrupted while waiting?
qa.a: The barrier is broken: the interrupted thread gets InterruptedException, all other waiting parties (and anyone who calls await later) get BrokenBarrierException. A timeout or an exception in the barrier action breaks it the same way. Recovery requires reset(). This all-or-nothing design keeps parties from continuing with an incomplete round.

qa.q: Why can a CyclicBarrier deadlock inside a thread pool?
qa.a: If the pool has fewer threads than barrier parties, the first tasks block in await() and occupy every worker; the remaining parties sit in the queue with no thread to run on, so the barrier never trips. Pool size must be at least the party count, or use Phaser / non-blocking composition.

qa.q: Phaser vs CyclicBarrier?
qa.a: Both support repeated rounds. Phaser allows parties to register and deregister dynamically, has numbered phases, lets a thread arrive() without waiting, supports custom termination via onAdvance, and can be tiered for very large party counts. CyclicBarrier has a fixed party count and a simpler API with a barrier action.

qa.q: Implement producer–consumer. Which approach would you use in production?
qa.a: By hand: a bounded buffer with synchronized + while-guarded wait() and notifyAll(), or ReentrantLock with notFull/notEmpty conditions. In production: a bounded BlockingQueue (ArrayBlockingQueue or a capacity-bounded LinkedBlockingQueue) with producers calling put/offer(timeout) and consumers calling take, run on an executor, with a deliberate shutdown (poison pill per consumer or interruption).

qa.q: How do you stop consumers in a producer–consumer system cleanly?
qa.a: Poison pills: after all producers finish (track with a CountDownLatch or join), enqueue one sentinel per consumer; FIFO order guarantees real items are processed first. Alternatives: shutdownNow() interrupts (drops queued work), or a volatile running flag with poll(timeout) that exits when the flag is false and the queue is empty.

qa.q: ArrayBlockingQueue vs LinkedBlockingQueue?
qa.a: ArrayBlockingQueue: fixed capacity, array-backed, a single lock for both ends, optional fairness, no per-item allocation. LinkedBlockingQueue: linked nodes, separate put and take locks so producers and consumers don't contend (higher throughput), but allocates a node per item and is unbounded by default — always pass a capacity.

qa.q: Why does the semaphore-based bounded buffer acquire the counting semaphore before the mutex?
qa.a: If a producer took the mutex and then waited on emptySlots, it would block while holding the mutex; the consumer needs that mutex to remove an item and release a slot, so both wait forever. Waiting on the counting semaphore first and locking only around the buffer mutation avoids the deadlock.

cheat.concurrency-cheatsheet:
Threads, lifecycle and interruption

  • Threads share the heap but each has its own stack; only start() creates a new thread — calling run() executes on the caller.
  • Six states: NEW, RUNNABLE, BLOCKED (monitor), WAITING, TIMED_WAITING, TERMINATED.
  • Interruption is cooperative: blocking calls throw InterruptedException and clear the flag, so restore it with Thread.currentThread().interrupt() or propagate.
  • Daemon threads don't keep the JVM alive and skip finally on exit; set an UncaughtExceptionHandler for visibility.

Java Memory Model: visibility, ordering, happens-before

  • Bugs come from atomicity, visibility and ordering; the JMM guarantees visibility only along happens-before edges.
  • Key edges: unlock → next lock, volatile write → later read, start(), join(), and transitivity.
  • volatile gives visibility and ordering, not atomicity: count++ on a volatile still loses updates.
  • Publish shared objects safely: final fields, volatile/atomic references, static initializers or a lock.

synchronized, intrinsic locks, wait/notify

  • Every object has a monitor; synchronized gives mutual exclusion plus visibility and is reentrant.
  • Prefer a private final lock object over locking this or the class.
  • Always call wait() in a while loop on the condition, holding the monitor; use notifyAll() when different kinds of waiters share it.
  • sleep keeps locks; wait releases the monitor.

Explicit locks: ReentrantLock, Condition, ReadWriteLock, StampedLock

  • ReentrantLock adds tryLock with timeout, interruptible locking, fairness and multiple Conditions; always unlock in finally.
  • Two Conditions (notFull, notEmpty) give targeted wakeups in bounded buffers.
  • ReentrantReadWriteLock allows many readers or one writer; downgrade is allowed, upgrade deadlocks.
  • StampedLock optimistic reads take no lock but must be validated; it isn't reentrant.

Atomics, CAS and LongAdder

  • Atomics use CAS retry loops: lock-free, so no deadlocks, but retries waste CPU under heavy contention.
  • LongAdder stripes a counter across cells and beats AtomicLong for write-heavy metrics.
  • ABA: a value changes A→B→A and CAS still succeeds; fix with AtomicStampedReference.
  • updateAndGet lambdas may run several times, so they must be side-effect free.

Executor framework and ThreadPoolExecutor

  • ThreadPoolExecutor order: core threads → queue → extra threads up to max → rejection handler.
  • newFixedThreadPool uses an unbounded queue (OOM risk) and newCachedThreadPool unbounded threads: build your own with a bounded queue, named threads and a deliberate rejection policy.
  • Size CPU-bound pools near the core count; I/O-bound ≈ cores × (1 + wait/compute), then measure.
  • submit() hides exceptions inside the Future; shut down with shutdown() + awaitTermination() then shutdownNow().

Future and CompletableFuture

  • thenApply maps, thenCompose flat-maps async calls, thenCombine merges two independent futures, allOf fans in.
  • Always pass your own executor for I/O; the default common pool is small and shared with parallel streams.
  • Handle failures with exceptionally/handle, unwrap CompletionException, and add orTimeout.
  • complete() / completeExceptionally() bridge callback APIs into futures.

Synchronizers: choosing the right tool

  • Semaphore limits concurrency; CountDownLatch waits for N events once; CyclicBarrier makes N threads meet repeatedly; Phaser does dynamic phases.
  • BlockingQueue is the producer–consumer tool; CompletableFuture composes async results without blocking.
  • Use a lock, not a semaphore, to protect shared state.
  • Pick by asking: limit, wait-once, meet-repeatedly, hand-off, or compose?

Under the hood: AbstractQueuedSynchronizer (AQS)

  • AQS = a volatile state changed by CAS + a FIFO queue of parked threads + template methods.
  • Exclusive mode backs locks; shared mode backs Semaphore, CountDownLatch and read locks.
  • state means hold count, permits or remaining count depending on the synchronizer.
  • Non-fair modes let arriving threads barge for throughput; fair modes serve strictly FIFO.

Semaphore in depth

  • Permits have no owner: any thread may release, which enables signalling but makes leaks and over-release easy.
  • Acquire first, then try { … } finally { release(); } — never acquire inside the try.
  • Prefer tryAcquire(timeout) for bulkheads so overload becomes a fast rejection, not a hang.
  • With virtual threads, a Semaphore is the standard way to cap pressure on databases and APIs.

CountDownLatch in depth

  • One-shot gate: waiters block until countDown() brings the count to zero; it can't be reset.
  • countDown() happens-before a successful await() return, so workers' results are visible.
  • Always count down in finally and await with a timeout, or one failed worker hangs the caller forever.
  • CountDownLatch(1) is a start gate that releases many threads at once.

CyclicBarrier in depth

  • N parties wait for each other; the last arrival runs the barrier action, then all proceed and the barrier resets.
  • Interrupt, timeout or an action exception breaks the barrier: everyone gets BrokenBarrierException; recover with reset().
  • A pool with fewer threads than parties deadlocks.
  • Latch = wait for events signalled by others; barrier = wait for each other, repeatedly.

Phaser and Exchanger

  • Phaser is a reusable barrier with numbered phases where parties can register and deregister at runtime.
  • arriveAndAwaitAdvance waits; arrive doesn't; onAdvance can terminate the phaser.
  • Exchanger swaps objects between exactly two threads, e.g. double buffering.
  • Tiered phasers reduce contention with thousands of parties.

Producer–Consumer: the complete guide

  • A bounded buffer gives backpressure: producers block when full, consumers block when empty.
  • By hand: while-guarded wait/notifyAll, or a lock with notFull/notEmpty conditions; in production: a bounded BlockingQueue.
  • Stop consumers with one poison pill per consumer after producers finish, or by interruption.
  • Never use an unbounded queue; never do slow I/O while holding the buffer's lock.

Synchronizers: rapid-fire Q&A and implement-it-yourself

  • You can build a semaphore from a lock + condition, a latch from synchronized + wait/notifyAll, and a barrier with a generation counter.
  • Semaphores aren't reentrant; latches can't reset; barrier actions run in the last arriving thread.
  • Fair semaphores prevent starvation of large acquire(n) requests at a throughput cost.
  • A generation counter stops a fast thread from slipping through the next barrier round.

Concurrent collections and ConcurrentHashMap internals

  • ConcurrentHashMap: CAS into empty bins, lock only the bin head, lock-free reads, cooperative resize, no nulls.
  • Use atomic per-key operations (merge, compute, computeIfAbsent) instead of get-then-put.
  • CopyOnWriteArrayList suits read-mostly listener lists; iterators never throw CME.
  • Know the BlockingQueue methods: put/take block, offer/poll return special values, timed variants wait.

ForkJoinPool, work stealing and parallel streams

  • Work stealing: each worker has a deque; idle workers steal old, large tasks from others' tails.
  • Fork one half, compute the other, then join; choose a sensible sequential threshold.
  • Parallel streams run on the shared common pool: use them only for large, CPU-bound, splittable work.
  • Avoid parallel streams with blocking I/O, LinkedList sources or shared mutable state.

ThreadLocal, leaks and ScopedValue

  • Each thread gets its own copy; values live in the thread's map, so pooled threads keep them forever.
  • Always remove() in finally, or you leak memory and leak data between requests.
  • InheritableThreadLocal goes stale with pools; propagate context explicitly (TaskDecorator, context propagation).
  • ScopedValue (final in JDK 25) is the immutable, bounded, virtual-thread-friendly replacement.

Virtual threads (Project Loom, JDK 21)

  • Virtual threads unmount from carrier threads when they block, making thread-per-request scale to millions.
  • They speed up blocking I/O, not CPU-bound work; don't pool them.
  • Bound downstream resources explicitly (Semaphore, connection pool size).
  • Pinning inside synchronized was fixed in JDK 24; on 21–23 prefer ReentrantLock around blocking calls.

Deadlock, livelock, starvation and how to debug them

  • Deadlock needs mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption and circular wait; break one (usually lock ordering).
  • tryLock with timeout and random back-off avoids both deadlock and livelock.
  • Diagnose with several thread dumps (jcmd <pid> Thread.print) and ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads().
  • Watch for thread-starvation deadlock: tasks blocking on subtasks queued in the same bounded pool.

Concurrency patterns: immutability, singleton, confinement

  • Immutability is the simplest thread safety: final class, final fields, defensive copies, or records.
  • Lazy singletons: double-checked locking needs volatile; the holder idiom and enums are simpler.
  • Thread confinement (one owner thread) needs no synchronization: event loops, Kafka consumers.
  • Other patterns: striped locks per key, single-writer, read-copy-update with AtomicReference.

Classic coding problems (asked in interviews)

  • Odd/even and ABC printing are turn-taking: a shared turn with wait/notifyAll, or semaphores passing a baton.
  • Producer–consumer with a BlockingQueue and poison pill is the production answer.
  • A thread-safe LRU needs an exclusive lock because get reorders a LinkedHashMap.
  • Token bucket: refill tokens by elapsed time under a lock, then take one.
